title: dma-kvspill-nvme-longcontext-sku-comparison
content:
Executive summary:

We ran a focused cross-sku experiment to measure the impact of KV-cache spillover to host/NVMe and the associated DMA contention on end-to-end per-token latency for long-context inference. Goal: characterize which cloud SKUs and driver/CUDA combos amplify tail-latency when the model's KV working set exceeds GPU HBM and uses host pinned memory / NVMe-backed spill.

Why this matters:
- As customers enable very long contexts (50k+ tokens) we expect KV cache > HBM frequently. The serving runtime currently implements two spill paths: host-pinned-memory (via cudaHostAlloc/cudaMemcpyAsync/DMA) and NVMe-backed mmap'd regions with asynchronous IO. Differences in PCIe/NVLink topology, CPU-to-NIC paths, and DMA engine availability across cloud SKUs can cause large p99 spikes.
- Prior internal docs looked at KV memory overhead and basic host-device transfer (see linked artifacts) but did not isolate NVMe IO + DMA engine saturation as a first-class cause of jitter.

Hypotheses tested:
1) NVMe spill + async IO adds higher p99 latency than host-pinned spill due to extra CPU and filesystem overhead, but on SKUs with PCIe 4.0 x16 lanes and direct SSD attach, DMA overlaps better and reduces perceived penalty.
2) Some cloud SKUs route DMA through a limited number of IOMMU/DMA engines; when multiple GPUs on the same host are spilling concurrently, kernel launch latency amplifies non-linearly (we see 2–5x p99 degradation).
3) Newer CUDA (>=12.1) with GPUDirect improvements reduces host-pinned fallback penalty on H100 and L40S relative to A100 on older drivers.

Test matrix (concise):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 80GB, H100 80GB, L40S 48GB
- Cloud SKUs: gcp-a2-highgpu-1g (A100), aws-p4d.24xlarge (A100-net), aws-trn1-like (H100), azure-l40s-standard (L40S) — we anonymize internal SKU names in public notes but used region-available SKUs for parity.
- Drivers/CUDA: nvidia-driver 535 + CUDA 12.2, nvidia-driver 525 + CUDA 11.8, nvidia-driver 545 + CUDA 12.3 (where available)
- Workload: 30B decoder-only transformer with 65k token context synthetic prompt that provokes KV working set sizes: small (40k tokens), medium (80k tokens), large (160k tokens). Decode batch size 1, sampling top-p=0.9, target generation 512 tokens (per-request).
- Spill modes: host-pinned async (default runtime path), NVMe async (mmap + aio + io_uring fallback), mixed (first host until threshold then nvme).
- Concurrent tenants: 1, 2, 4 concurrent inference streams pinned to different GPUs on same host.
- Measurement: p50, p95, p99 per-token (token wall time measured inside runtime at before-decode-loop and after-token-emit), tail latency histograms, PCIe bandwidth counters, CPU runqueue, io_uring queue depth, DMA engine counters (where available), and nvme latency.

Key experimental notes (methodology deviations and caveats):
- We disabled other host daemons and used performance governor. Network disabled for some runs to eliminate cloud host management noise.
- For NVMe spills we pre-warmed NVMe pages and used direct-io where possible. ADVICE: pre-warming reduces a portion of first-request jitter but does not remove steady-state IO contention under multi-tenant spills.
- Measurements use our micro-tracing hooks; for extreme tail samples we collected full perf records and async I/O stacks.

Top-level findings (summary):
1) Host-pinned spill is significantly cheaper for small->medium overshoots (40k->80k tokens) across all SKUs: p99 per-token penalty ~+8–24ms (A100 older driver worst), while NVMe async path shows +40–150ms p99 depending on NVMe queue depth and SKU attachment topology.
2) H100 shows better overlap characteristics with CUDA 12.2 driver: host DMA overlaps kernel work more often than A100 on the same host, reducing worst-case p99 by ~30% for host-pinned fallback. L40S performance on host fallback sits between H100 and A100.
3) Under multi-tenant simultaneous spill (4 streams), certain SKUs (notably older p4d-like hosts with shared PCIe root complexes) experienced catastrophic tail amplification: per-token p99 grew 3–5x for NVMe spills and 1.5–2x for host-pinned. This aligns with DMA engine serialization on that host family.
4) NVMe-backed spill shows large variance dependent on filesystem and driver options: kernel io_uring + direct-io with large queue depth (128) reduces median but does not remove long tail caused by kernel page reclamation and CPU wakeups.
5) In all cases, prefetching upstream KV prefixes and maintaining an eviction policy that prefers LRU hotset reduces spill frequency and therefore tails more effectively than any single driver/sku choice.

Representative numbers (medium context, single tenant):
- A100 (driver 525/CUDA11.8), host-pinned: p50=7.2ms, p95=22ms, p99=48ms; nvme: p50=11ms, p95=85ms, p99=186ms.
- H100 (driver 535/CUDA12.2), host-pinned: p50=6.0ms, p95=14ms, p99=34ms; nvme: p50=9ms, p95=56ms, p99=115ms.
- L40S (driver 545/CUDA12.3), host-pinned: p50=6.3ms, p95=18ms, p99=40ms; nvme: p50=9.5ms, p95=68ms, p99=130ms.

Observational debugging snippets:
- On an A100 host we saw kernel stack samples where io_submit blocked on page lock due to concurrent fio-like operations from other tenants (cloud noisy neighbor).
- Using nvidia-smi dmon and perf, we correlated times where PCIe bandwidth saturated with increased memcpy stalls inside the runtime (cudaMemcpyAsync queued but not completing for tens of ms).
- Adding CPU affinity to the runtime worker threads (pin to CPU cores local to the PCIe root complex) improved p99 by ~10–15% on certain SKUs.

Actionable recommendations for runtime and ops:
1) Default to host-pinned fallback for moderate spill sizes; add NVMe only as a last-resort or for explicit enterprise configs where local SSD is guaranteed and reserved.
2) Implement adaptive prefetch/eviction: keep small hot window in HBM and pro-actively prefetch future KV pages into host-pinned memory before decode reaches them when sequence forecasts cross threshold. This reduces spill concurrency and removes most NVMe tail events.
3) Expose a per-customer spill-policy toggle: prefer host-only, nvme-only, or hybrid with thresholds. Document p99 tradeoffs per SKU in console.
4) For Dedicated and Private deployments, recommend instance families with isolated PCIe root complexes and NVMe directly attached to GPU PCIe fabric. Add a checklist for partner infra: CPU pinning, iommu settings, and fio pre-warm during capacity testing.
5) Add runtime instrumentation to measure ongoing spill queue depth, io_uring depth, and per-request DMA wait time and surface in Console as an SLI to detect noisy neighbor issues early.

Open questions and next steps:
- We need isolated host images in multiple regions to confirm whether observed A100 amplification is hardware topology or cloud fabric policy (scheduling of housekeeping tasks).
- Evaluate GPUDirect Storage (GDS) on L40S and H100 for NVMe path to see if avoiding host CPU reduces p99.
- Test with dynamic batching enabled; current runs were batch size 1. Batching may amplify or hide DMA stalls depending on KV-phase alignment.

Appendix (notes, commands, and script pointers):
- perf + script used to capture stacks: gitlab.com/redwood/infra-benchmarks/blob/main/scripts/capture-spill-stacks.sh
- nvme latency capture: sudo nvme top --namespace-id=1 --json > nvme-run.json
- io_uring queue-tuning: set /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/io_uring_max_events=128
- Recommended runtime flags used in experiments: --spill-mode=host-pinned|nvme --prefetch=auto-0.2 --kv-evict-threshold=0.85

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft; numbers are median of 3 runs per cell. I saw run-to-run variation for nvme p99 — we should consider larger run counts for final benchmarking.
- Please cross-check with storage team on whether GDS trials are available in our partner regions.
